sources.title: James Forsyth, A History of the Peoples of Siberia, Cambridge University Press excerpt
sources.note: Scholarly overview emphasizing Siberia as a vast region of many Indigenous peoples, languages, ecologies and histories rather than one society.

sources.title: W. K. Matthews, Palaeoasiatic Languages, Cambridge University Press
sources.note: History and components of the geographic Palaeoasiatic classification, including Chukotko-Kamchatkan, Yukaghir, Nivkh and Ket.

sources.title: Glottolog 5.3, Chukotko-Kamchatkan
sources.note: Current linguistic classification and warning that proposed links with Nivkh are insufficient to establish a genealogical relationship.

sources.title: Migrations and interactions in prehistoric Beringia: the evolution of Yakutian lithic technology
sources.note: Dated Syalakh, Belkachi and Ymyakhtakh sequences, mobile hunting and fishing economies, pressure-flaked blades, pottery, harpoons and regional terminology.

sources.title: Radiocarbon chronology of Neolithic and Bronze Age cultures in Yakutia
sources.note: Ninety-two radiocarbon dates revising Ymyakhtakh, Ust-Mil, Ulakhan Segelennyakh and Sugunnakh chronologies in Yakutia.

sources.title: Kyordyughen Site, Ymyiakhtakh Culture, Yakutia: An Interpretation of Burial Rite
sources.note: Late Neolithic burial, dismembered remains, possible sacrifice and cautious debate about warriors and social differentiation.

sources.title: The population history of northeastern Siberia since the Pleistocene
sources.note: Ancient genomes showing repeated migrations and mixture, including approximately 3,000 to 2,000-year-old samples from Chukotka and the Okhotsk coast.

sources.title: Crossroads of Continents: Cultures of Siberia and Alaska
sources.note: Smithsonian synthesis of regional archaeology and later lifeways, including dwellings, clothing, tools, watercraft, food, art and gendered tasks.

sources.title: Crossroads Alaska: Native Cultures of Alaska and Siberia
sources.note: Smithsonian museum synthesis stressing distinctive peoples, shared Beringian exchange and the limits of modern political borders.

sources.title: Archaeology in Northeast Asia: On the Pathway to Bering Strait
sources.note: Smithsonian catalog of specialist studies on pottery, obsidian, Ekven, Chukotka, Kamchatka, Sakhalin and maritime dating.

sources.title: Archaeological Sites of Kamchatka, Chukotka, and the Upper Kolyma
sources.note: Smithsonian catalog of surveyed sites, cultural layers, fortified settlements, burials, petroglyphs and regional chronologies.

sources.title: Obsidian Provenance Studies on Kamchatka
sources.note: Geochemical sourcing of Kamchatkan obsidian, multiple sources per site and transport or exchange distances reaching hundreds of kilometers.

sources.title: A Study of Finds from Excavation I at Suchu Island, the Lower Amur
sources.note: Stratigraphy, dwellings, pottery, stone tools, minerals, portable art and ritual objects across Lower Amur occupations.

sources.title: Spatial Distribution of Finds on the Eastern Outskirts of Poltse I
sources.note: Plans of ten dwellings, central hearths and the distribution of hundreds of ceramic vessels, with cautious trade interpretation.

sources.title: A Radiocarbon Chronology of the Poltse I Settlement on the Amur River
sources.note: Fifteen new dates placing the settlement mainly from the later first century BCE through the second century CE and linking it to regional exchange.

sources.title: Reindeer Imagery in the Making at Ust-Polui in Arctic Siberia
sources.note: Ritual center dated about 260 BCE to 140 CE, carved imagery, perishable tools, dog sacrifice and early evidence for transport-reindeer relationships.

sources.title: Storing fish? A dog isotopic biography and Iron Age food preservation in the Russian Arctic
sources.note: Stable isotopes, fishing seasonality and evidence that Lower Ob communities mass-harvested and froze fish for people and dogs.

sources.title: Decorated Birch-Bark Artifacts from the Ust-Polui Sanctuary
sources.note: Direct study of decorated perishable artifacts preserved at the Lower Ob ritual complex.

sources.title: Early Iron Age Ceramics from the Ust-Polui Ritual and Production Center
sources.note: Multidisciplinary technological study of pottery manufacture at the northwestern Siberian ritual and production center.

sources.title: Modern Siberian dog ancestry was shaped by several thousand years of Eurasian-wide trade and human dispersal
sources.note: Ancient dog genomes and archaeological evidence for exchange, ironworking, transport and changing Siberian networks.

sources.title: Evolution of the Okvik and Old Bering Sea culture as a major transition
sources.note: Bering Strait settlement, marine technology, labor specialization, social ranking and symbolic communication, used to audit the atlas exclusion of Chukotka.

sources.title: Ancient Koryak Culture
sources.note: Okhotsk-coast permanent settlements, maritime economy, dwellings and iron links with Yakutia and Bering Sea traditions.

sources.title: Opisthorchiasis in infant remains from medieval Zeleniy Yar
sources.note: Direct twelfth to thirteenth-century parasite evidence for undercooked fish, infant diet and health in northwestern Siberia.

sources.title: Medieval mummies of Zeleny Yar burial ground in Western Siberia
sources.note: Interdisciplinary study of twelfth to thirteenth-century birch-bark cocoons, bodies and genetic diversity, with representativeness warnings.

sources.title: Rich Burials of Children at Zeleny Yar, Northwestern Siberia
sources.note: Child burials with varied containers, clothing, ornaments, tools and cautiously inferred high rank.

sources.title: The changing environment, Writing, Society and Culture in Early Rus
sources.note: Distinguishes script-bearing imported objects from local literacy in northern forest regions.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Arctic Lands and Peoples
sources.note: Institutional overview of distinct Arctic peoples, environments, seasonal resources and technologies.

scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.
Agent researched a disjoint batch; integration and structural checks are not independent historical certification.
Imported border coordinates remain unchanged. Historical events and map coverage are distinguished in prose; see batchIdentityNotes for conflicts.

proposedOverrides.summary: Atlas umbrella for many distinct Siberian communities from 2000 BCE to 1279 CE; never one people.

batchIdentityNotes: The exact id paleo-siberian-hunter-gatherers is preserved only as an atlas display key for circa 2000 BCE to 1279 CE.
Paleo-Siberian or Palaeoasiatic is a later geographic umbrella, not one demonstrated language family, state, people or ancient self-name.
The atlas polygon and the linguistic umbrella have different extents; the map excludes Chukotka before 1279 while including many western and central regions.
Regional archaeological labels such as Ymyakhtakh, Ust-Mil, Sugunnakh, Poltse and Okhotsk contexts are not treated as automatic ethnic aliases.
Repeated geometry across centuries records basemap reuse. Tiny coordinate changes and the reversible 800 western jump are not narrated as migrations.
The 700 Tungus seam and 1279 siberians seam are changing atlas vocabulary, not synchronized cultural replacement or political succession.
Later ethnography is explicitly labeled comparison and is never projected unchanged into the target interval.
No contemporaneous written sample is supplied because no common target language or securely attributable self-authored text exists for the umbrella record.
